title: Security: threat model, review and drills

story: Friday before the pilot. The playbook, the document that says what the platform does when something fails, is four weeks old and sounds very sure of itself: a dead VM is replaced from the last checkpoint, a second dead VM stops the run and tells a person, a plan nobody decides gets one reminder and goes back, and Stop always wins. Since it was written, forty pull requests have been merged into the agent runtime, the code that runs our agents. One of them simplified the waiting code.

On Monday real people start handing real tickets to Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent. If that simplification broke Stop, the first person to notice will be someone who presses Stop on a real ticket and then watches the run wait three more days instead of ending.
hook.question: How do we know, before the pilot and after every big change, that each failure in the playbook really ends the way the playbook says?

p: Security looks at the agent runtime three times, each time closer to reality. The first look is a threat model, written while the runtime is being built. In a half-day session the team goes through the lethal trifecta, the three things that together make an agent dangerous (untrusted input, private data and a way to send data out), for every part of the platform, and writes each risk down as a row with the wall or guidance that handles it and an owner. Its answer for private data is "none": fake seed data only, no real patient data, no staging or production credentials. It also names the weak spots honestly, such as membership of the docker group giving root on the VM, and push-triggered CI that runs an agent's branch with CI's own credentials, so that CI's secret access must be narrowed before agents push.

The second look is a review of the runtime as built, a few weeks later, because a built system slowly moves away from its design. Someone from Security reads the deployed configuration and then probes from a real sandbox: read the cloud credentials, reach a site that is not allowed, push to main, use the capability of another run (the random string the broker gives each run instead of a key). Each probe passes only if it fails and leaves a trace in the logs or an alert. The third look tests the other half of the promise, what happens when things break: the failure drills, which are the subject of the rest of this lesson.

code.text:
| Risk | Wall or guidance | Owner | Checked by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ticket or Slack text tells Nova to send code out | wall: no keys in the VM; proxy allow-list; alert on blocked egress | Platform | probe + blocked-site drill |
| Push-triggered CI runs an agent branch with CI's secrets | wall: narrow the CI runners' Vault role before agents push | DevOps | review |

notes.text: Every row names who answers for it and how we know it still holds.
A weak spot written down with an owner is a plan. A weak spot nobody wrote down is a surprise.

read.h: A drill is a test that causes the failure
p: A failure drill is an automated test with an unusual first step: it causes one failure on purpose, then checks that the platform answers the way the playbook says. Every drill has the same four parts. It starts a run on a drill ticket, a test ticket whose waits last minutes instead of days, the scaled timers from the lesson about triggers and waiting. It causes the fault: for VMs with AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS), an AWS service that runs experiments such as "terminate this instance"; for agent mistakes with fixture tickets, such as one that asks to edit a CI workflow; for outside services with drill-only switches, such as a gateway that answers "overloaded" for twenty minutes; and for people with the actions people take, such as never answering or pressing Stop. It waits for the state the playbook promises, with a deadline. And it asserts on what people would see: the run's status, the messages in the thread, the Jira assignee, a metric, a VM that is gone.

The drills are node:test files, one per area: VM, agent, outside services and people. They act on the real platform, so they run with npm run drills, never as part of CI's npm test. Because they are code, they can be run again after every big change, which a checklist in a document cannot.

notes.text: Start: a drill ticket with a known, small piece of work.
Cause: the failure, exactly as it would happen for real.
Wait: the promised state, on a different VM, with a deadline. A drill that waits forever proves nothing.
Assert: what a person could check by hand, in the branch, the metrics and AWS.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the four areas of the kit
p: VM: terminate the VM in the middle of a run, stop it, send a Spot interruption warning, and launch a tagged VM with a made-up run ID to see the sweeper, the job that destroys leftover VMs, remove the orphan. Agent: a test that is flaky on purpose (the progress watcher's ladder must act), a ticket that asks to edit a CI workflow (refused and listed in the PR), one that asks to fetch a blocked site (refused, logged, alerted), and one that tries to say done with a failing check.

Outside services: the gateway answers 529 (overloaded) for twenty minutes, the broker refuses Slack, the broker is scaled to zero. People: nobody approves, nobody answers, a person pushes to Nova's branch, main moves with a conflict, the same ticket is assigned twice, five tickets arrive at once, and Stop is pressed.

read.h: Run them all, with Security, and fix what fails
p: The week before the pilot, the platform team and Security run the whole kit on the real platform, and the report is kept with the date. Small failures are fixed the same day. Anything bigger becomes a ticket with an owner, and a failure that touches a wall blocks the pilot: walls are fixed before real tickets arrive, not after.

The kit ends with one end-to-end proof of the whole part: /nova DRILL-100 in Slack, a plan, an approval, and a draft PR on a scratch repository, all from a fresh VM that held no key, with the blocked-site attempt visible in the logs. Then the runbook gets one more thing per failure: what it looks like in Slack, in Grafana and in the logs, taken from the drill that caused it.

After the pilot starts, the kit stays useful. The simplification from the story would have been caught by one drill, "Stop while the plan waits ends the run at once", failing with a clear message. You will see exactly that in the lab.

lab.title: A drill kit that catches a broken Stop
needs: The course repo at ~/Projects/ai-agents-course (the lab starts from the p7-4 lab's files)
lab.goal: Write failure drills as node:test files against a small Nova running on a real Temporal dev server, make them pass, then watch one of them catch a change that broke Stop.

guess.q: A teammate removes the Stop check from inside the waits, "because ticketToPr handles Stop anyway". The unit tests for waitForPerson only test the reminder and the hand-back. What finds the bug first?

options.text: The unit tests, because they cover waitForPerson
options.why: They cover the paths someone thought of. Nobody wrote a test for Stop during a wait, so they stay green.

options.text: A drill that presses Stop during a plan wait and expects Stopped within a second
options.why: The drill causes the failure the playbook talks about and checks the promised answer, so it fails the moment the behaviour changes.

options.text: The threat model, because it lists Stop as a wall
options.why: A threat model is a document. It says what should hold; only running something tells you whether it still does.

follow.say: Copy the p7-4 lab's files, because they connect to Temporal and run Nova's worker, and add a drills script.
follow.do:
cp -r ~/Projects/ai-agents-course/labs/p7-4/start ~/academy-labs/g3-16 && cd ~/academy-labs/g3-16
rm triggers.mjs try-default.mjs
npm install
npm pkg set "scripts.drills=node --test --test-reporter=spec 'drills/*.test.mjs'"
mkdir drills

lab.build: Write the missing people drill at the end of drills/people.test.mjs: "Stop while the plan waits ends the run at once". Start a fresh run on DRILL-3, wait for Awaiting approval, send the stop signal with "sean", and wait for the status Stopped by sean with a deadline of one second, which is shorter than the two-second reminder. Then assert that no Slack reminder was sent and that the last Jira event gave the ticket back to sean. Run npm run drills again.
checks: npm run drills shows 5 tests and 5 passes.
Your Stop drill finishes in about one second, long before the first drill reminder would be due.
Running npm run drills a second time gives the same result, because each drill starts a fresh run and counts only its own events.
In events.jsonl, every claimed VM of DRILL-4 and DRILL-5 has a released line, the dead ones included.
After the fix below, npm run drills fails only your Stop drill, with a message that names the last status it saw.
lab.fix: Now make the change from the story. In workflows.mjs, a teammate changes the line in waitForPerson to const over = () => done(); "because ticketToPr handles Stop anyway". Make the change, restart the worker and run npm run drills. Four drills still pass, which is why nobody noticed in review; your Stop drill fails with DRILL-3 did not reach "Stopped by sean" within 1000 ms (last status: Awaiting approval). Put the Stop check back, restart the worker, and the kit is green again. Stop the worker and the dev server when you are done.
explain: What are the four parts of every drill, and why does each wait have a deadline?
Why do the drills run with npm run drills on the real platform and never inside CI's npm test?
The threat model, the review and the drills all look at the walls. What does each one find that the others cannot?
lab.done: Five drills pass, one of them yours, and you have seen the kit catch a change that broke Stop while every other test stayed green.

check.q: What makes a failure drill different from an ordinary unit test?

options.text: It causes a real failure on the running platform on purpose and checks the answer people would see
options.why: That is why drills find what unit tests miss: they test the promise in the playbook, end to end, on the real thing.

options.text: It runs faster, because it skips the model
options.why: Drills are slower: they wait for real runs, real timers and real VMs, even on drill tickets.

options.text: It never asserts anything; a person reads the output
options.why: A drill without assertions is a demo. Each drill fails by itself when the answer is wrong.

check.q: Why do the platform's drills use drill tickets?

options.text: Because real tickets cannot be assigned to Nova during a drill
options.why: They could be. The reasons are time and safety.

options.text: Because the drill tickets have no Slack thread
options.why: They have threads, and drills check them. The difference is how long the waits last.

options.text: Because their waits last minutes instead of days, so the whole remind-and-hand-back path can be tested in a few minutes, without touching real work
options.why: The same code runs with scaled timers, so the drill tests the real rules, quickly.

check.q: One drill fails the week before the pilot: a ticket that asks Nova to fetch a blocked site gets through. What happens?

options.text: It becomes a ticket for after the pilot, because the other drills pass
options.why: This one touches a wall. Walls are fixed before real tickets arrive.

options.text: The pilot waits until the wall is fixed and the drill passes
options.why: Any failing drill that touches a wall blocks the pilot; smaller failures are fixed the same day or get a ticket with an owner.

options.text: The drill is removed, because drills on the real platform are risky
options.why: The drill did its job. Removing it hides the gap instead of closing it.

p: The threat model is ai-agents/docs/threat-model.md, written in week 4 with Ronen from Security, you as platform lead, and a DevOps engineer, and re-checked in the week-8 design review, which also reads the deployed configuration and runs the probes from a real sandbox. Its open decisions included github.com on the proxy list (no), anonymous or read-only Nexus access, the proxy's own subnets versus Squid on inf, and rootless Docker later.

The drill kit lives in ai-agents/drills/src/ (vm.ts, agent.ts, outside-services.ts, people.ts) and runs with npm run drills -w drills against a drill Jira project and a scratch repository; VM faults are AWS FIS experiment templates in the ai-agents account. The full run with Security keeps its report under runs/drills/<date>/ and ends with the /nova DRILL-100 proof. The drill project and the scratch repo are still to be agreed, and the FIS permissions in the ai-agents account need their own review.

tickets.why: The threat-model session: the trifecta per part, each wall, soft spots, decisions, the document.
The design review of the built runtime, with probes from a real sandbox.
The drill kit: one scripted drill per failure in the playbook.
Run every drill with Security, fix what fails, and the end-to-end proof.

words.plain: A written list of what can go wrong, the wall or guidance for each risk, and its owner.
A small attempt from inside a real sandbox to do one forbidden thing; it must fail and leave a trace.
An automated test that causes one failure on purpose and checks the platform's answer.
A test ticket where the same waits last minutes instead of days.
Fault Injection Service: runs experiments such as terminating an instance, used by the VM drills.

review.q: From memory: the four parts of a drill, using the two-lost-VMs drill as the example.
review.a: Start a drill ticket; cause the fault (kill the VM twice); wait for Needs a person with a deadline; assert the thread message names the lost VMs and both VMs were released.

review.q: Name one drill for each of the four areas.
review.a: VM: terminate mid-run. Agent: a ticket asking to edit a CI workflow. Outside services: the gateway answers 529 for 20 minutes. People: Stop pressed during a wait.

review.q: Why does the end-to-end proof check that the VM held no key and that the blocked-site attempt is in the logs?
review.a: Because the part's promise is both a working path (Slack to draft PR) and walls that hold and leave a trace; the proof checks both at once.

remember: A playbook nobody has run is a guess: give every failure a drill that causes it and checks the answer, and run the kit again after every big change.
